newsitem.title: SPAIN: FOCUS-Spain cuts key rate after inflation tumbles.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Spain cuts key rate after inflation tumbles.

text.p: The Bank of Spain sanctioned its second interest rate cut of the year on Friday in what analysts considered a vote of confidence in the Spanish economy.

The central bank lowered its key money market rate by 25 basis points to 5.75 percent one day after Spain reported that consumer inflation dropped to 2.5 percent year-on-year in February from 2.9 percent in January.
Economy Secretary Cristobal Montoro attributed the reduction to improved inflation and said more cuts may lie ahead.
"As inflation and the public deficit confirm their declines, we will certainly see more interest rate declines," he said.

"We have been getting a series of good news, which together with the labour market reform agreement, builds confidence in Spain and confirms us as one of the strongest candidates for EMU (European Economic and Monetary Union) launch," he said.
The conservative Popular Party government has made Spanish participation in EMU the cornerstone of its European Policy and has launched a fiscal clean-up effort to ensure it makes the grade.
This interest cut had been widely expected, with seven of ten economists surveyed by Reuters predicting the move given that inflation had sunk to levels not seen since January 1969.
The Bank of Spain has been easing monetary policy since December 1995, which it shaved 25 percentage points off the peak rate of this business cycle, bringing it down to nine percent.
But a minority of economists had said worries about the peseta and other concerns would keep the central bank from cutting.

"It was obviously a good inflation number," said Craig Schute, fixed-income analyst at Bear Stearns. "I thought they might be worried about foreign exchange markets. But they've bashed all that aside."
"It was a confident move by the bank of Spain," Schute said.
Still, the Bank of Spain may have held back from a large rate reduction amid caution about the peseta's previous wobbles.

"The Bank of Spain has responded with its usual caution and has only cut 25 basis points. Although most CPI components are performing well, services have a resistance at 3.4/3.5 percent and this invites caution," said Carmen Hernansanz, economist at Merrill Lynch Espana.
Although the government lost no time pressing its claim for lower rates, some analysts were skeptical and markets were little impressed.

Stocks and bonds, harried by worries of interest rate increases out of the United States, both fell. At 1315, the IBEX index of 35 stocks had fallen 1.04 percent to 5,508.48 while long-bond futures were off nearly half a point.
And analysts added that the Bank of Spain move could pose a danger for financial markets in front of both a possible rate hike by the U.S. Federal Reserve later this month and peristent EMU jitters.
"I have the feeling they took a risk on board, as the peseta could react badly in the following days," said Giovanni Polastri at 4CAST in London.
At 1340 the peseta was trading at around 84.92/93 per mark -- weaker than yesterday's closing level of 84.84/88.
